summary.text: Writing \(T_n=n(n+1)/2\), the defining sum gives \(a_{n+1}=(2^n-1)a_n+2^{T_n}\); for odd \(p\), Fermat’s theorem and \(T_{n+2(p-1)}-T_n=(p-1)(2n+2(p-1)+1)\) make both coefficients periodic modulo \(p\), while the vanishing multiplier at \(n=2(p-1)\) resets the value to \(a_1=1\), so induction gives the claimed period. For \(p=2\), the same recurrence shows directly that every positive-index term is congruent to \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_k=\frac{k(k+1)}2=\binom{k+1}{2}.
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{T_k}\prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1),\qquad n\geq 1.
\]
(We may also define the same expression for \(n=0\), in which case the sum is empty and \(a(0)=0\).)

We first derive a recurrence for this sequence. In the expression for \(a(n+1)\), every summand with \(0\leq k<n\) is obtained from the corresponding summand in \(a(n)\) by adjoining the last factor \(2^n-1\) to its product. The remaining summand, corresponding to \(k=n\), has an empty product, hence equals \(2^{T_n}\). Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n+1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{T_k}\left(\prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1)\right)(2^n-1)+2^{T_n}\\
&=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{T_n}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]
In particular, directly from the defining sum, \(a(1)=1\): its only summand has \(k=0\), exponent \(T_0=0\), and an empty product.

We prove that for every prime \(p\), with
\[
M=2(p-1),
\]
one has
\[
a(n+M)\equiv a(n)\pmod p
\tag{2}
\]
for every \(n\geq 1\). We separate the cases \(p\neq2\) and \(p=2\).

First suppose that \(p\) is an odd prime. Put \(q=p-1\), so \(M=2q\). Since \(p\nmid2\), Fermat's little theorem gives
\[
2^q=2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p.
\tag{3}
\]
It follows that powers of \(2\) whose exponents differ by a multiple of \(q\) are congruent modulo \(p\): for all nonnegative integers \(r,s,L\) satisfying \(r=s+Lq\),
\[
2^r=2^s(2^q)^L\equiv2^s\pmod p.
\tag{4}
\]

We now examine the two quantities occurring on the right side of recurrence (1). For the coefficient \(2^n-1\), since \(M=2q\), equation (4) gives
\[
2^{n+M}-1=2^{n+2q}-1\equiv2^n-1\pmod p.
\tag{5}
\]
Thus the coefficient sequence in (1) is periodic modulo \(p\) with period \(M\).

The inhomogeneous term is periodic with the same period. Indeed, a direct calculation with triangular numbers gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{n+M}-T_n
&=\frac{(n+2q)(n+2q+1)-n(n+1)}2\\
&=q(2n+2q+1).
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
T_{n+M}=T_n+q(2n+2q+1).
\]
The difference is a nonnegative multiple of \(q=p-1\), so (4) implies
\[
2^{T_{n+M}}\equiv2^{T_n}\pmod p.
\tag{7}
\]

It remains to establish one initial equality before propagating it with recurrence (1). We claim
\[
a(M+1)\equiv a(1)\pmod p.
\tag{8}
\]
Apply (1) at the index \(M\):
\[
a(M+1)=(2^M-1)a(M)+2^{T_M}.
\tag{9}
\]
By (3),
\[
2^M=2^{2q}=(2^q)^2\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
so the coefficient \(2^M-1\) in (9) is zero modulo \(p\). Also, formula (6) with \(n=0\), or a direct calculation, gives
\[
T_M=T_{2q}=q(2q+1).
\]
Hence (3) again yields
\[
2^{T_M}=(2^q)^{2q+1}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Reducing (9) modulo \(p\), we therefore obtain
\[
a(M+1)\equiv0\cdot a(M)+1\equiv1\equiv a(1)\pmod p,
\]
which proves (8).

We can now prove (2) by induction on \(n\geq1\). The base case \(n=1\) is exactly (8). Suppose for some \(n\geq1\) that
\[
a(n+M)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\tag{10}
\]
Using recurrence (1) at indices \(n+M\) and \(n\), and then using (5), (7), and (10), we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n+M+1)
&=(2^{n+M}-1)a(n+M)+2^{T_{n+M}}\\
&\equiv(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{T_n}\\
&=a(n+1)\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the induction advances from \(n\) to \(n+1\), proving (2) for every \(n\geq1\) when \(p\) is odd.

It remains to treat the prime \(p=2\). In this case we show the stronger statement
\[
a(n)\equiv1\pmod2\qquad(n\geq1).
\tag{11}
\]
We already know \(a(1)=1\), so this holds at \(n=1\). Suppose \(n\geq1\) and \(a(n)\equiv1\pmod2\). Since \(n\geq1\), the number \(2^n\) is even, so
\[
2^n-1\equiv1\pmod2.
\]
Also \(T_n=n(n+1)/2\) is positive for \(n\geq1\), and therefore \(2^{T_n}\) is even. Reducing recurrence (1) modulo \(2\) now gives
\[
a(n+1)\equiv(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{T_n}\equiv1\cdot1+0\equiv1\pmod2.
\]
This proves (11) by induction. For \(p=2\), the proposed period is
\[
2(p-1)=2.
\]
Both \(n\) and \(n+2\) are at least \(1\), so (11) gives
\[
a(n+2)\equiv1\equiv a(n)\pmod2.
\]

Combining the odd-prime case with the case \(p=2\), for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq1\) we have
\[
a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]
Equivalently, their remainders upon division by \(p\) are equal:
\[
a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\bmod p=a(n)\bmod p.
\]
Thus the sequence modulo every prime \(p\), starting at its first term, is purely periodic with a period dividing \(2(p-1)\), as claimed.
